title: Two Reasons to Agree
scopeNote: This keeps the two-route model with both routes reported separately, and the conditions that move each. The continuous parameter sliders, the participant task and the simulation of a hundred individuals behind the group rate are in the longer version. Conditions are offered as presets so the learner compares rooms rather than tuning coefficients, and every condition run stays in the table.
summary: Six fictional conditions on one task. Taking the audience away removes about twenty-one points of agreement when the display is easy and about eleven when it is ambiguous, because a different route is doing the work.
learningObjectives: Distinguish normative from informational influence by what moves each.
Explain why making a response private separates the two.
Explain why one dissenter changes far more than the arithmetic suggests.
Explain why a conformity rate is not a finding without a context.
Recognise identification with the group as a term the classic account lacks.
interactionTypes: a prediction before any condition is seen
six conditions the learner runs in any order
each run kept in a growing comparison table
the two routes reported separately rather than as one rate
a guided comparison that applies one manipulation in two rooms
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No task is administered to the reader.
dataStatus: A fictional display and a small two-route model whose parameters are printed on the page. Nothing here reproduces the stimuli, procedure or data of any published study, and no figure is an estimate of anything.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Conditions are ordinary buttons, and one already run is marked with aria-disabled rather than the disabled attribute so it stays reachable and readable. Every figure is in a real table with row and column headers as well as in the chart, and each bar in the chart is labelled with its value and with the name of its route in words, so the two routes are never told apart by colour alone. The chart description lists every condition run with both its routes and its total. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: Agreement on a critical round is two independent routes, each of which can produce it, combined as one minus the product of their complements. The normative route is a constant multiplied by unanimity, by whether anybody is watching, by identification with the group and by how clear the norm is; the informational route is a constant multiplied by how ambiguous the task is, by the standing of the majority and by unanimity. Two features carry the teaching and both are checked in the test suite rather than asserted. Whether anybody is watching appears only in the normative term, so making the response private leaves the informational route numerically identical, which is what makes it the manipulation that tells the two apart: it removes 21.3 points of agreement on the easy display and 11.3 on the ambiguous one, because in the second room most of the agreement was never normative. And unanimity is a step rather than a headcount, taking the normative multiplier from 1.00 to 0.30 at the first dissenter, so a majority of four to one collapses the rate while a second dissenter changes comparatively little. Identification is the social-identity amendment the classic two-route account does not contain, and an outgroup majority produces a much lower rate with the informational route untouched. Every figure quoted in the feedback and the notes is computed from the parameters rather than written in. This is a teaching model and not a replication: the parameters are printed so they can be argued with, and the page states that the classic findings are of their time and place, that conformity is not a defect being measured, and that a group average conceals a distribution.
readmeTopic: how to tell normative from informational influence, and why a conformity rate needs a room
